prompt: Which of the following experimental procedures will effectively reduce the effect of random errors when measuring a time interval?
options: Checking whether the stopwatch displays 0.00 s before starting the measurement.
Repeating the timing measurement five times and calculating the mean.
Replacing the digital stopwatch with a clock that has a coarser scale.
Calibrating the stopwatch against an accurate laboratory frequency standard.

answer.explanation: Repeating measurements and calculating a mean allows random fluctuations to cancel partially, directly reducing the effect of random error.

distractor_explanations: Checking the initial zero reading detects a zero (systematic) error, not random error.
Correct. Repeated independent measurements and calculating the mean reduce the effect of random errors.
Using a coarser scale increases reading uncertainty and reduces resolution.
Calibration corrects systematic rate/clock errors, not random human reaction variations.
hints: Which procedure deals with unpredictable scatter?
Remember that random errors cancel out in the average of repeated readings.
solution: Repeating the timing measurement five times and calculating the mean reduces the effect of random errors.
teacher_walkthrough: Identify the goal: reducing the effect of random error.
Random errors vary unpredictably in sign and magnitude.
Averaging several independent readings allows positive and negative variations to cancel.
Checking zero and calibrating address systematic errors.

provenance.independence_statement: Authored to test proper experimental intervention for random errors.
